items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public health law and the social services law, in relation
to requiring single-purpose day camps to ascertain whether an employee or
volunteer is listed on the state sex offender registry pursuant to article
six-C of the correction law
items.lawCode: Amd Art 13-B Art Head, §§1392 & 1393, add §1394-c, Pub Health L; amd §424-a, Soc Serv L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S3966          REVISED 02/17/2021

SPONSOR: REICHLIN-MELNICK
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law and the social services law, in
relation to requiring single-purpose day camps to ascertain whether an
employee or volunteer is listed on the state sex offender registry
pursuant to article six-C of the correction law

 
PURPOSE:

To ensure the safety and welfare of our children by requiring that
single-purpose day camps check the sex offender registry for all poten-
tial employees and volunteers; and to require all camps check the state-
wide central register for child abuse and maltreatment to ascertain if
an employee or volunteer is the subject of a child abuse and maltreat-
ment report on file with the state.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one amends the article heading of article 13-B of the public
health law to include single-purpose day camps within the applicability
of the article.

Section two adds a new subdivision, 3-a, to § 1392 of the public health
law to provide a definition for a "single-purpose day camp."

Section three amends § 1393 of the public health law to require single-
purpose day camps to obtain a permit prior to operation. This section
also specifies the circumstances under which a permit should be issued.

Section four amends the public health law by adding a new section,
1394-c, requiring single-purpose day camps to ascertain whether an
employee or volunteer is listed on the state sex offender registry prior
to the date the employee or volunteer begins work at such camp.

Section five amends § 424-a of the social services law by Adding a new
paragraph, d-2, to subdivision 1 requiring all camps that fall under the
provisions of article 13-B of the public health law, to check whether
any employee or volunteer is on file with the statewide central register
of child abuse and maltreatment.

Section 6. Effective on the one hundred eightieth day after it shall
become law.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Protecting the safety and welfare of our children is of the utmost
importance. Summer camps are an important part of our children's experi-
ence. However, not all camps currently fall under Department of Health
Regulations. Single-purpose day camps are not required to check their
employees or volunteer's background. We must ensure that we protect
children whether they attend an outdoor summer camp or a single-purpose
day camp. Requiring these camps to check the sex offender registry and
the statewide central register of child abuse and maltreatment will
further protect our children's safety.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
2019-20: S0152 referred to Health
2017-18: S4082 Passed Senate
2015-16: S1750 - Passed Senate
2013-14: S1986 referred to Health
2011-12: S5239 - referred to Health

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the one hundred eightieth day after it
shall have become a law.

BILL NUMBER: S3966A

SPONSOR: REICHLIN-MELNICK
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law and the social services law, in
relation to children's non-regulated camps

 
PURPOSE:

To ensure the safety and welfare of our children by requiring that
single-purpose day camps check the sex offender registry for all poten-
tial employees and volunteers; and to require all camps check the state-
wide central register for child abuse and maltreatment to ascertain if
an employee or volunteer is the subject of a child abuse and maltreat-
ment report on file with the state.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill amends the public health law by adding a new
section, 1394-c, requiring the operators of children's non-regulated
camps to ascertain whether an employee or volunteer is listed on the
state sex offender registry prior to the date the employee or volunteer
begins work at such camp.

Section two of the bill five amends § 424-a of the social services law
by Adding a new paragraph, d-2, to subdivision 1 requiring all camps
that fall under the provisions of article 13-B of the public health law
or a children's non-regulated camps as defined in section 398(f) of the
general business law, to check whether any employee or volunteer is on
file with the statewide central register of child abuse and maltreat-
ment.

Section three provides that this shall be effective on the one hundred
eightieth day after it shall become law.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Protecting the safety and welfare of our children is of the utmost
importance. Summer camps are an important part of our children's experi-
ence. However, not all camps currently fall under Department of Health
Regulations. There are certain types of camps that are not required to
check their employees or volunteer's background because those camps are
not regulated by the Department of Health. We must ensure that we
protect children even if they attend a non-regulated camp. Requiring
children's non-regulated camps, as defined by § 398(f) of the general
business law, to check the sex offender registry and the statewide
central register of child abuse and maltreatment will further protect
our children's safety.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2019-20: S0152 - referred to Health
2017-18: S4082 - Passed Senate
2015-16: S1750 - Passed Senate
2013-14: S1986 - referred to Health
2011-12: S5239 - referred to Health

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the one hundred eightieth day after it
shall have become a law.

B.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S3966B

SPONSOR: REICHLIN-MELNICK
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law and the general business law, in
relation to children's non-regulated camps

 
PURPOSE:

To ensure the safety and welfare of our children by requiring that
single-purpose day camps and camps regulated by DOH check the national
and state sex offender registry for all potential employees and volun-
teers.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one amends the public health law by adding a new section 1394-c,
requiring the operators of children's non-regulated camps to ascertain
whether an employee or volunteer is listed on the state and national sex
offender registries prior to the date an employee or volunteer begins
work at such camp.

Section two amends paragraph (a) of subdivision 2 of section 398-f of
the general business law to omit relevant language from the written
notice that non-regulated camps must send to parents.

Sections three, four and five amend sections 1392a, 1394a and 1394b to
require camps regulated by DOH to check whether an employee or volunteer
is listed on the state and national sex offender registries prior to the
date the employee or volunteer begins work at a camp.

Section six provides the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Protecting the safety and welfare of our children is of the utmost
importance. Summer camps are an important part of our children's experi-
ence. However, not all camps currently fall under Department of Health
(DOH) regulations. There are certain types of camps that are not
required to check their employees or volunteer's background because
those canips are not regulated by the Department of Health. We must
ensure that we protect children even if they attend a non-regulated
camp. Requiring children's non-regulated camps, as defined by § 3980) of
the general business law, to check the national and state sex offender
registries will further protect our children's safety.

This bill also strengthens protections for children attending camps
regulated by DOH by requiring them to check the national sex offender
registry. Under current law, these camps are only required to check the
state sex offender registry.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.
 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the one hundred eightieth day after it
shall have become a law.

summary: Requires children's non-regulated camps to ascertain whether an employee or volunteer is listed on the state sex offender registry pursuant to article six-C of the correction law and the national sex offender registry using the national crime and information center, established under the Adam Walsh child protection and safety act of 2006 (42 U.S.C. 16901 et seq.).
